title: Wiz Discloses CosmosEscape, and Practitioners Debate What Customers Could Have Done
gist: Wiz disclosed CosmosEscape, a Gremlin-query sandbox escape in Azure Cosmos DB that exposed a platform-wide 'Master Key' able to read/write any tenant's database; Microsoft blocked the entry point in two days but needed until July 2026 to remove the shared secret, and practitioners debated who bears responsibility for a flaw customers had zero ability to mitigate.

insights.claim: Cosmos DB compiled Gremlin queries into .NET code under sandbox restrictions that did not sufficiently account for .NET reflection, letting a crafted Gremlin query escape the sandbox and achieve code execution on the DB Gateway.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Shows how a compiler-level abstraction gap in a query-language sandbox becomes an RCE vector in a multi-tenant managed database; worth probing for any vendor whose service compiles a query DSL into a general-purpose runtime.
insights.locator: The chain began with a crafted query against a Gremlin database

insights.claim: The sandbox escape exposed what Wiz calls the Cosmos Master Key, a platform-wide secret capable of retrieving the primary key of any Azure Cosmos DB account and enumerating databases filtered by subscription and tenant identifiers.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A single platform-wide secret architecture converts one sandbox bug into total cross-tenant compromise; investors and buyers evaluating managed-database vendors should ask directly about shared-key vs. per-tenant-key design.
insights.locator: Escaping the sandbox gave code execution on the DB Gateway

insights.claim: The blast radius of the Cosmos DB flaw extended to Microsoft's own backends, since Cosmos DB underpins internal services including Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Copilot.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Microsoft's own flagship products depend on the same compromised substrate as customers, showing internal dependency concentration risk inside Microsoft's stack, not just customer-facing risk.
insights.locator: The blast radius extended to Microsoft's own backends

insights.claim: Wiz reported CosmosEscape to Microsoft on November 20, 2025; Microsoft acknowledged it the same day and blocked the vulnerable Gremlin entry point with a hotfix within two days, but did not finish removing the platform-wide master key until July 2026 when it completed a new credential model across all regions.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The eight-month gap between 'entry point blocked' and 'secret actually removed' is the real signal for judging vendor security disclosures — a patched CVE headline can mask months of unresolved architectural exposure.
insights.locator: Wiz reported the issue on November 20, 2025

insights.claim: The DB Gateway used the master key to fetch each account's private key before forwarding requests, so eliminating the key required rebuilding the credential model of a service Microsoft itself depends on, explaining why full remediation took roughly six months longer than the initial hotfix.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Deep architectural fixes (rearchitecting a shared-secret credential model) take vastly longer than patching the discovered entry point, a useful proxy for estimating true remediation timelines after any hyperscaler disclosure.
insights.locator: Commenter phatskat noted that the gateway had used the master key

insights.claim: Practitioners pushed back on criticism of the slow six-month fix, arguing the scale involved — a service serving Microsoft itself and tens of thousands of customers — made an overnight rewrite of the database query execution engine unrealistic.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Frames remediation-speed complaints against genuine engineering scale, a useful calibration when assessing whether a vendor's fix timeline is negligence or proportionate to system complexity.
insights.quote: It's a major service for themselves and tens of thousands of customers; you don't vibe code yourself a new database query execution engine overnight.
insights.locator: Another commenter, delfinom, made the same point about scale

insights.claim: Practitioners argued CosmosEscape sits entirely on the provider's side of the shared responsibility model because there was nothing a Cosmos DB customer could have done differently to prevent it — the flaw lived entirely in Microsoft's infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A clean case study proving some vulnerability classes are entirely unmitigable at the customer configuration layer; enterprise due diligence on cloud vendors should probe multi-tenant key architecture, not just customer-side settings.
insights.quote: This is the kind of vulnerability that doesn't show up in any shared responsibility model diagram. As a Cosmos DB customer, there is nothing we could have done differently to prevent this; it lives entirely in Microsoft's infrastructure

insights.claim: A commenter challenged Microsoft's 'no evidence of customer impact' assurance by questioning who actually verifies a provider-side fix worked, since customers have no independent way to confirm remediation of a flaw entirely inside the provider's infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Highlights an audit-verification gap recurring across cloud vendor risk assessment: customers cannot independently confirm remediation of provider-side flaws and must simply trust vendor statements.
insights.quote: Rejecting the premise: who says they fixed it properly?
insights.locator: Commenter dointheatl put that doubt directly in the HN thread

insights.claim: One camp argued for backing up critical data to a second cloud provider or on-premises as protection against hyperscaler-side flaws; a counter camp argued hypervisor codebases are equally buggy and typically patched worse by ordinary organizations than by a hyperscaler, while conceding that hyperscaler failures are worse in blast radius when they do occur.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Frames the multi-cloud/on-prem hedging debate concretely: the tradeoff isn't bug frequency but blast-radius severity when a hyperscaler-side flaw does surface.
insights.quote: The problem is, when it goes wrong, it really goes wrong with the hyperscalers.
insights.locator: Commenter maceinjar countered that hypervisor code bases

insights.claim: A typical on-premises estate does not expose its management APIs to the internet and does not carry cross-tenant pivot risk, making it a fundamentally different threat model from hyperscaler multi-tenancy rather than simply a smaller-scale version of the same risk.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'hyperscalers get hacked too, so what's the difference' argument — cross-tenant pivot via an internet-exposed management API is a hyperscaler-specific risk class absent on-prem.
insights.quote: It's a different threat model though.
insights.locator: Commenter LLMsMustUpvoteThis then narrowed the comparison

insights.claim: No CVE identifier and no CVSS score have been issued for CosmosEscape, which is unusual for a vulnerability Wiz itself describes as critical.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Absence of standard vulnerability scoring for a 'critical' finding is itself a data point worth tracking when comparing Microsoft's disclosure rigor against industry norms.
insights.locator: No CVE identifier and no CVSS score

insights.claim: No MSRC advisory was published for CosmosEscape, unlike for two prior Cosmos DB vulnerabilities in the same service — ChaosDB in 2021 and CosMiss in 2022 — leaving Microsoft's account resting solely on statements given to Wiz and to reporters rather than a formal advisory.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A break from Microsoft's own precedent on prior Cosmos DB incidents is a specific, trackable signal of degraded disclosure rigor for a 'critical' finding.
insights.locator: No MSRC advisory, unlike ChaosDB in 2021 and CosMiss in 2022

insights.claim: Neither Wiz nor Microsoft stated when the vulnerable engine and signing-key path entered production or what period the access-log review covered, so Microsoft's assurance of 'no evidence of customer impact' has an undefined denominator.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A reusable skepticism heuristic for any vendor breach disclosure: 'no evidence of impact' is meaningless without a stated exposure window and log-retention scope.
insights.locator: No stated exposure window, since neither Wiz nor Microsoft says

insights.claim: The practical takeaway for platform teams evaluating any managed multi-tenant service is not a patch to apply but a question to ask the vendor: where does the platform hold a credential that spans tenants, and what would removing it cost?
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Gives security and platform teams a concrete, reusable due-diligence question for evaluating any managed multi-tenant vendor, not just Azure Cosmos DB.
insights.locator: For platform teams, the practical takeaway is not a patch to apply
